item.title: India weighs an AI rulebook against the compliance cost for startups
item.description:
India is weighing an AI governance framework covering deepfakes, data security and algorithmic accountability, including whether strict compliance would price early-stage startups out of the market. Antara Gupta of AIM spoke with Rahul Agarwalla, managing partner at SenseAI Ventures, Rohit Kumar, founding partner at The Quantum Hub, and Vishal Ranjan, founder of Claight. The discussion is framed around graded rules rather than a blanket rule, how liability could be split between model makers and application builders, what the EU AI Act and GDPR teach India, and whether India should chase frontier models. No speaker's conclusion is established.

Key points

  • India is weighing a framework covering deepfakes, data security and algorithmic accountability.
  • The open question is whether strict compliance would price early-stage AI startups out of the market.
  • Antara Gupta spoke with Rahul Agarwalla of SenseAI Ventures, Rohit Kumar of The Quantum Hub, and Vishal Ranjan of Claight.
  • The subjects include who is liable when AI agents go wrong, graded rules, a split between model makers and application builders, the EU AI Act and GDPR, and whether India should chase frontier models.
  • Further named subjects, without recorded conclusions, are watermarking, the online gaming ban, hallucinations, rogue agents, copyright and training data, safe harbors for startups, and enterprise AI.

item.title: Oracle and AstraZeneca use AI to match patients to clinical trials
item.description:
Oracle and AstraZeneca are using AI to match patients to clinical trials faster and to cut the cost of drug development. Oracle Health is pushing healthcare AI from patient portals to Fusion Claw agents, which let customers build their own agents. Amit Raja Naik, senior editorial producer for live shows at AIM, spoke with Seema Verma, executive vice president and general manager of Oracle Health and Life Sciences, at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas. What Verma said is not established beyond the subjects of that conversation.

Key points

  • Oracle and AstraZeneca are using AI to match patients to clinical trials faster and to cut drug-development cost.
  • Oracle Health's stated range runs from patient portals to Fusion Claw agents that customers can build themselves.
  • Amit Raja Naik spoke with Seema Verma at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas about the AstraZeneca partnership and where Oracle's healthcare business goes next.
  • The named subjects also include electronic health records, drug discovery, hospital operations, and hospitals in India.
  • No remarks by Seema Verma are established beyond those subjects.

item.title: EkaCare's voice scribe is headed to public hospitals under Ayushman Bharat
item.description:
The National Health Authority has selected EkaCare to implement an AI scribe in India's public healthcare system. The company will deploy an ambient voice scribe that turns doctor-patient conversations into structured records by capturing symptoms, medical history, diagnoses and treatment plans, with the aim of cutting the administrative burden on clinicians. The work is part of bringing modern tools into the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission. The scribe supports more than 15 Indian languages. The headline spells the company Ekacare.

Key points

  • The National Health Authority has selected EkaCare for an AI scribe in public healthcare, including public hospitals.
  • The body spells the company EkaCare. The headline spells it Ekacare.
  • The scribe captures symptoms, medical history, diagnoses and treatment plans from the conversation.
  • The deployment is described as part of the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission.
  • Support is for more than 15 Indian languages. No facility count or start date is given.

item.title: OpenAI's Control Room is meant to stop a job that leaves its authorized bounds
item.description:
OpenAI's Control Room is a system for managing risk by monitoring and halting unauthorized model behavior. It tracks AI workloads, assigns a unique ID to every job, and lets researchers intervene when a model acts outside its authorized parameters. Stop instructions are the safeguard against unpredictable actions. The headline says a suspicious training job can be cut off within 35 seconds. That timing is not repeated in the body, and suspicious is not defined.

Key points

  • Control Room monitors and halts unauthorized AI model behavior.
  • Every job gets a unique ID. Researchers can intervene when a model acts outside authorized parameters.
  • Stop instructions are described as the safeguard.
  • The headline says a suspicious training job can be cut off within 35 seconds. The body does not restate the 35 seconds.
  • No customer and no date are named.

item.title: Google.org's $2.3 million screening grant, cut down to a short
item.description:
Google.org is putting 2.3 million dollars into a Pune startup so health workers can be sent to high-risk neighborhoods instead of screening everyone. The short gives the grant and the method. It does not repeat the tuberculosis pilot counts from Wednesday's longer report, and its description does not print the company name.

Key points

  • The grant is 2.3 million dollars from Google.org, plus 200,000 dollars in Google Cloud credits and technical support, to expand an AI disease-screening platform.
  • The description says the app is offline, in local languages, and built for frontline health workers. It tells them where to go. It uses government health data and Google's Earth AI models to flag high-risk zones of about 300 metres.
  • The spoken extract adds local factors: settlement density, rainfall and flooding. It then says the app plans household visits. The auto-caption's last noun is "roots," which is not a clean word.
  • The description calls it "a Pune startup" and does not name it. The auto-caption renders a name close to "Franc.ai" and an app close to "MAI Netra." Wednesday's report spelled the company Froncort.AI on the lower third and the app mAI-Netra, and the automatic caption of that report garbled the company name. This short does not show the spelling.
  • Wednesday's report also gave the Maharashtra tuberculosis comparison, the cost figures, and the caveat that the tool has not been shown to find more patients. Those numbers are not in this short.

From the video

The anchor is the same unnamed man in a white shirt and glasses, at a laptop against the skyline. hq1.jpg puts a title card over a glass building with a Google mark. The card reads "Google Backs an AI That Finds the Uncounted Sick." The burned-in fragment is "Pune startup that wants." maxresdefault.jpg is an aerial view of turquoise water under "AI models and local." hq3.jpg is a view of Earth from orbit under "factors like." item.title: Auto parts face up to 25 percent US duty, and the EU zero-duty line has no signed text
item.description:
Indian auto parts face duty of up to about 25 percent in the United States, a February framework that promised relief is still not final, and a commerce-minister line on zero EU duty by March or April has no signed text behind it. The player length is 46 seconds. The opening line picks up Wednesday's car-export report. The Front Page take at the end was not in the wording that came back.

Key points

  • The narration opens with exporters having a tariff problem as well. Indian auto parts face duty of up to about 25 percent in the United States.
  • A trade framework in February promised relief. It is still not final. A burned-in caption reads "in February promised."
  • The commerce minister said the EU should offer zero duty by March or April. The description calls him the commerce minister. The burned-in caption spells the name Goyal, in the line "Goyal also said the EU." The auto-caption says "Mr. Goyel." Wednesday's export report named Piyush Goyal.
  • The short calls that EU timing an expectation stated on stage. It says Front Page's research has not found any signed text for the claim.
  • The anchor says an exporter cannot plan a business around a figment of hope. The auto-caption spells that word "vigment." The caption on screen at that moment is "a business around."
  • The retrieved wording ends as he turns to the Front Page take. The take itself was not in the text that came back, so it is not summarized here.

From the video

The anchor is the same unnamed man in a white shirt and glasses. maxresdefault.jpg shows a white-bearded man in a dark vest facing a blond man in a dark suit, under "Goyal also said the EU." hq1.jpg is the same meeting under "in February promised." hq3.jpg is a man with glasses in a light shirt and dark vest at a podium, under "a business around." Neither man in the upper frame is named on that frame. The full video file was not downloaded.
